title: AIP-C01 Skill 1.5.1: Chunking Documents for Better Retrieval
html:
AIP-C01 Skill 1.5.1: Chunking Documents for Better Retrieval

A hands-on lab comparing fixed-size, hierarchical and semantic chunking in Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Task 1.5, post 1 of 7.

[IMAGE: cover-1-5-1.png — alt: "Skill 1.5.1: Chunking documents for better retrieval"]

AIP-C01 Hands-on Labs · Domain 1 · Task 1.5: Design retrieval mechanisms for FM augmentation · Post 1 of 7. Hands-on lab, about 40 minutes.

Task 1.4 decided where vectors live. Task 1.5 is about getting the right passages out of them. It starts before any search: with how documents are cut into chunks. Cut a policy in the wrong place and a chunk says “Returns are accepted within 14 days only” without saying which products that applies to. The search finds it, the model quotes it, and the answer is wrong for drills.

How Task 1.5 is covered

[IMAGE: t1-5-post-map.png — alt: "Task 1.5 in seven posts: skills 1.5.1, 1.5.2, 1.5.4, 1.5.5 and 1.5.6 as labs, 1.5.3 as notes, then exam notes"]

What AWS says

The exam guide's fifth Domain 1 task is Task 1.5: Design retrieval mechanisms for FM augmentation. Its first skill:

Skill 1.5.1: Develop effective document segmentation approaches to optimize retrieval performance for FM context augmentation (for example, by using Amazon Bedrock chunking capabilities, Lambda functions to implement fixed-size chunking, custom processing for hierarchical chunking based on content structure).

What it means in plain words

  • Document segmentation: chunking. Splitting documents into pieces that are each embedded and retrieved on their own.
  • Amazon Bedrock chunking capabilities: the built-in strategies a knowledge base offers: default, fixed-size, hierarchical, semantic, or none.
  • Lambda functions for fixed-size chunking: your own chunking code, run as a custom transformation during ingestion or in your own pipeline.
  • Hierarchical chunking based on content structure: using the document's own headings and sections to decide where to cut, and keeping small pieces linked to their larger section.

[IMAGE: t1-5-1-strategies.png — alt: "Five chunking options in Knowledge Bases: default, fixed-size, hierarchical, semantic and none, with parameters and best use"]

What we're going to do

  1. Chunk a short returns policy in plain Python two ways: fixed-size and by structure. No AWS needed.
  2. Create two knowledge bases from the same document, identical except for chunking.
  3. Ask both the same question and compare what reaches the model.

What you'll learn

  • Why chunk boundaries change answers, not just search scores.
  • How hierarchical chunking matches on small chunks but returns large ones.
  • When to use semantic chunking, no chunking, or your own Lambda function.
  • Why the chunking strategy is a decision you make once per data source.

What you'll need

  • Time and cost: about 40 minutes, under US$0.20 if you clean up the same day
  • Region: us-west-2
  • Access: Python 3.10+ with boto3; an S3 bucket in us-west-2; permission to create Bedrock knowledge bases; Titan Text Embeddings V2
  • Files: github.com/prasanth2006z/aip-c01-labs, folder domain-1/task-1.5/skill-1.5.1-chunking

The lab

Part 1: Chunk in code

returns-policy.md has four sections: general terms, garden equipment, cordless power tools, clearance. The garden and power tool sections use almost the same sentences (“Returns are accepted within … days”) with different numbers. That's what makes chunking matter.

Step 1: Fixed-size chunks

python chunkers.py fixed

The function cuts the text into windows of 30 words that overlap by 5, ignoring headings on purpose. This is the logic a Lambda function would run for fixed-size chunking. Look at where the cuts fall: some chunks start halfway through a section, with no heading to say what they're about.

Step 2: Chunks by structure

python chunkers.py structure

This time each ## section becomes a parent chunk, and each parent is split into small child chunks that carry their heading:

[Garden equipment] Returns are accepted within 14 days only. A restocking fee ...

Step 3: Compare

python chunkers.py compare

For a question about returning a hedge trimmer and the fee, the fixed-size method hands the model whichever 30-word window matched best, which may be cut mid-section. The structure method matches on the small child, then hands the model its whole parent: the garden section with its heading, its window, its fee and its fuel rule. Small for matching, large for answering.

Part 2: Two knowledge bases

Step 4: Upload and create

aws s3 cp returns-policy.md s3://your-bucket-name/chunking-lab/

In the Bedrock console create two knowledge bases from s3://your-bucket-name/chunking-lab/, with Titan Text Embeddings V2 and a quick-created S3 Vectors store. Only the chunking differs:

[IMAGE: t1-5-1-lab-settings.png — alt: "Lab settings: kb-chunk-fixed with fixed-size 40 tokens and no overlap, kb-chunk-hier with hierarchical parent 400, child 40, overlap 20"]

Forty tokens is deliberately tiny so the problem shows on a one-page document. With real documents you'd use a few hundred.

Step 5: Sync and compare

Sync both data sources, then:

export KB_FIXED=XXXXXXXXXX KB_HIER=XXXXXXXXXX
python compare_kbs.py
python compare_kbs.py "Can I return a clearance drill?"

The script asks each knowledge base for five results. From kb-chunk-fixed you get five short fragments, some from the wrong section, none with its heading. From kb-chunk-hier you get fewer than five results, and each one is a whole section. That's expected: several child chunks matched, but they share a parent, and the knowledge base returns each parent once.

The second question is the interesting one. A drill is a cordless power tool (90 days), but it's on clearance (final sale). Only an answer that sees both sections, with headings, gets it right.

Choosing a strategy

  • Default: about 300 tokens, keeps sentences whole. Fine to start with.
  • Fixed-size: uniform documents, predictable chunk count and cost.
  • Hierarchical: long, structured documents where answers need the surrounding section.
  • Semantic: long text without clear headings. A model finds where meaning changes, which costs extra at ingestion.
  • None: each file is already one complete unit, such as one FAQ answer per file. You lose page-number metadata in citations.
  • Custom Lambda transformation: your own rules, such as splitting on a contract's clause numbers or adding metadata to each chunk. The knowledge base calls your function during ingestion.

The strategy is set when the data source is created and can't be changed afterwards. To switch, create a new data source and ingest again.

Common pitfalls

  • Fewer results than asked for from a hierarchical knowledge base: normal. Children that share a parent collapse into one result.
  • Trying to edit chunking on an existing data source: not possible. Create a new one.
  • Making fixed chunks bigger to fix missing context: it dilutes precision. Use hierarchical chunking instead.
  • Markdown headings lost: check the parsing option; the default parser keeps text, but advanced parsing (a foundation model or Bedrock Data Automation) handles tables and complex layouts better.

Clean up

  • Delete both knowledge bases.
  • Delete the S3 vector buckets that quick create made (S3 console → Vector buckets).
  • Delete the chunking-lab/ objects and the two knowledge base service roles.

What to remember

  • Chunk boundaries decide what the model reads, so they change answers.
  • Answers miss surrounding context → hierarchical chunking (small children for search, parents for context).
  • No clear structure → semantic chunking. Pre-split files → no chunking.
  • Custom splitting rules or per-chunk metadata → a Lambda custom transformation.
  • The strategy is fixed per data source; changing it means a new data source and re-ingestion.

The exam scenarios for this skill are in post 7 of this task: Task 1.5 Exam Notes.

References
